title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
raw_text: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade. As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure. Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity. These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid. The grid’s backbone Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. title: GPT-6.1 Terra
raw_text: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). Loes Damhof opened the discussions by exploring the importance of public spaces in an increasingly accelerated society. She invited participants to imagine libraries as places where people can slow down, reflect and explore possibilities — spaces that create room for what lies between the present and the future. Martin Berendse introduced OBA Next, an ambitious project that approaches the library of the future not as a finished building, but as an evolving concept. Its temporary laboratory, opened in 2025 in partnership with TUMO, is already experimenting with new ways of learning, creating and engaging young people, ahead of the planned permanent library in 2030. Building on this theme, Pegor Papazian, co-founder of TUMO, presented a different vision of education, drawing on his experience of working with teenagers and young adults. title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
raw_text: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers , go , javascript , jeff-lindsay , shot-scraper

The assistant will help researchers to review papers more effectively, support them in navigating manuscripts, and identify areas that may need closer attention so they can spend more time on the questions that require specialist scientific judgement. The partnership brings together Springer Nature’s expertise in managing peer review and Google DeepMind’s frontier Gemini models. Building on Google’s experience in developing proven agentic research tools like ScholarPeer and Deep Review , the new assistant helps reviewers analyse large amounts of text, charts, and figures. The prototype assistant currently being tested will help re-envision peer review as an interactive experience that uses AI to empower scientific experts while keeping expert human judgment at the centre of the process. title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
raw_text: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide . A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl . These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling. We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines. title: Information Integrity in the Age of AI: Brazil’s Approach to Trustworthy Government Publications
raw_text: By Carla Maria Martellote Viola, Senior Researcher, Brazilian Institute of Information in Science and Technology (Ibict), Brazil As governments increasingly use Artificial Intelligence (AI) to draft, organize and deliver information, a central question is becoming unavoidable: how can the integrity of government publications be protected when generative AI is part of the information-production process? In Brazil, this issue is gaining relevance alongside the Brazilian Artificial Intelligence Plan (PBIA 2024–2028), “AI for the Good of All”, which combines technological development with social inclusion, protection of rights, information integrity and responsible AI governance [1]. Information integrity involves more than factual correctness. It depends on information being accurate, complete, reliable and sufficiently contextualized, while its origin and transformations remain traceable. In institutional environments, these attributes support transparency and public trust and help reduce the risks of error, manipulation and bias. Provenance is especially important because it allows the origin, trajectory and modifications of information to be identified and its authenticity to be assessed [2]. For government publications, where citizens may rely on official information to understand rights, policies and public services, these requirements acquire particular significance. title: From Beirut to Byblos: LAU Libraries as a Beacon of Hope
raw_text: By Caline Trad , IFLA-GIOPS -Information Coordinator and Dr. Jordan Srour, Interim Dean of Libraries and Information Resources, LAU Running three academic libraries across two campuses is not easy in normal times. The Lebanese American University Libraries are at the heart of our campuses; they are the space where students go to study, to meet, to learn, to explore, to create, to print or to just relax. With so much activity anything can and does happen on an average day…now add a war. LAU’s response to the renewal of Israeli hostilities on 2 March 2026, followed standard protocols: a rapid move to online learning . While moving learning online sounds easy it belies a reality of stress and anxiety with students afraid that their grades will be impacted because their bandwidth falters. Against this backdrop, the LAU Libraries made a commitment to remain open to ensure that all learners could come to campus to access stable internet and electricity. Again, not an easy decision. Opening the libraries meant requiring staff to be present on campus – even in the face of streets that were crowded with displaced Lebanese, fuel prices that multiplied, and drones that circled – and still circle – overhead. War altered the meaning of librarianship inside the three LAU libraries. Unique in the design of the Riyad Nassar Library (RNL) in Beirut, is the fact that it doubles as an airstrike shelter. title: From North to South: Lebanon Rising from the Ashes
raw_text: By Caline Trad , IFLA-GIOPS -Information Coordinator Lebanon has always been much more than a country – from North to South it is a cradle of civilization, a mosaic of faiths and a land of resilience. Lebanon’s identity is woven with pluralism, with 18 sects recognized among Christian, Islam and Druze communities. This balance is also reflected in its political system, where at the highest level of government is a Christian president and a Sunni Muslim Prime Minister, emblematic of coexistence. This diversity, though often tested, is a source of strength and cultural richness. Throughout its long history, Lebanon has offered the world treasures of intellect and spirit: from the Phoenicians who carried trade and culture across the Mediterranean, to Gibran Khalil Gibran whose words turned Beirut into a beacon of inspiration, to Fairuz whose voice is the heartbeat of a nation. On a modest stretch of just 10,452 square km, mountains guarding over generations, posts welcoming travelers, and its people rising after every storm form the land of resilience where the Lebanese spirit never dies. From Byblos, where the first alphabet was born and took shape, to the cedar forests praised in scripture, Lebanon has stood as a sanctuary of saints and prophets, a land where churches and mosques rise side by side, and where faith and culture intertwine. raw_text: The first day of the Metropolitan Libraries Conference (MetLib 2026) in the Netherlands brought together library professionals from around the world to explore some of the most pressing questions facing our cities and societies. The key themes of the conference were introduced during the opening speeches and an inspiring keynote by artist Julia Janssen , focusing on the growing influence of technology on our lives. During our visit to The Hague Public Library, the director Sam Hermans , welcoming participants on behalf of the G4 cities organising the conference, emphasised that technology is already transforming the future of our cities. In this changing environment, libraries must remain places of connection, bringing people together and strengthening communities. In her thought-provoking keynote, Julia Janssen explored how algorithms increasingly shape our everyday lives, often without us even realising it. Through four examples from her artistic work, she demonstrated how digital technologies can reinforce the power of profit-driven corporations and gradually undermine our ability to think critically and question the systems around us. One of her most compelling messages was the need to demystify artificial intelligence — perhaps starting by calling it what it really is: automation . Worms mate in man's eyes, get plucked out right before larvae burst out
raw_text: After two months of discomfort, a man in South Korea went to an eye clinic where doctors pulled 11 living, wriggling worms from his eyes. They apparently made the most of their time on the man's peepers; at the time of extraction, many of the female worms were pregnant. The man narrowly avoided having them spew their loads of living larvae directly into his eyes. The man in this case was a 71-year-old crop farmer. He told doctors that for the previous two months he had the sensation of having something stuck in both his eyes, which were also red and blurry. When ophthalmologists took a look, they quickly saw the problem: multiple mobile, whitish roundworms. His eyes were not in good shape either, as one might expect. The blood vessels in the membrane over the eye, the conjunctiva, were enlarged, making his eyes look red. And the cells of his cornea—the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye—had eroded, potentially after the helminths' hanky-panky. According to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine , the doctors gave the man a topical treatment to numb his eyes and then began plucking out the worms one by one with fine forceps. They collected 11 adult worms, which ranged in size from 11 to 22 mm. Read full article Comments

title: Meet the real-life Scottish surgeon who inspired Sherlock Holmes
raw_text: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created one of the most beloved fictional detectives of all time in Sherlock Holmes, spawning countless novels, films, TV series, and so forth featuring the sleuth. Far fewer people know about the real-life inspiration for Holmes: a renowned surgeon at Scotland's University of Edinburgh named Joseph Bell, who taught Doyle when the author was still a young medical student. Bell is the subject of a new, eminently readable biography, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes , by medical historian Lindsey Fitzharris. A noted science communicator with a fondness for the medically macabre, Fitzharris published a biography of Scottish surgical pioneer Joseph Lister, The Butchering Art , in 2017—a great, if occasionally grisly, read. She followed up with 2022’s The Facemaker: A Visionary Surgeon’s Battle to Mend the Disfigured Soldiers of World War I , about a WWI surgeon named Harold Gillies who rebuilt the faces of injured soldiers. In 2020, Fitzharris hosted a documentary for the Smithsonian Channel, The Curious Life and Death Of… , exploring famous deaths, ranging from drug lord Pablo Escobar to magician Harry Houdini. Fitzharris performed virtual autopsies, experimented with blood samples, interviewed witnesses, and conducted real-time demonstrations in hopes of gleaning fresh insights. Starting at $699, the 8th-gen iPad mini price has gone up, but there are some big changes. Apple says the refreshed 8th-gen iPad mini marks the most significant update ever for its petite tablet, featuring an OLED screen and the A20 Pro chip that we first saw in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. The new iPad mini has roughly the same footprint as the 2024 release, but the display is slightly larger thanks to a 24 percent reduction in bezel thickness. The device is almost a full millimeter thinner than the last iPad, coming in at just 5.4 mm. The chassis is also IP67 rated for water and dust protection. The 7th-Gen iPad mini didn't have any official IP rating. The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display (up from 8.3 inches) moves on from the IPS technology of the last-gen device to adopt OLED. That means dapper blacks and a much higher peak brightness—1,200 nits versus just 500 nits for the previous mini. It can also manage 1-nit minimum brightness so as not to sear your retinas in a dark room. There will also be a nano-textured matte display option. The display experience on the new mini should be much more in line with what we've come to expect from Apple's Pro-level devices. Read full article Comments

title: ICE plan to buy robot dogs spurs protest from hundreds of Boston Dynamics employees
raw_text: Hundreds of employees at the US robotics firm Boston Dynamics signed a petition calling for executives to halt a sale of the company’s robot dogs to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement—but executives stood by the deal, while saying the robots would not be weaponized. On September 25, the Department of Homeland Security contract awarded $1.3 million to a Connecticut company called Radeco to provide ICE with modified versions of Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robots. But Boston Dynamics workers sent the petition letter with more than 300 signatures—half of them anonymous—to the company’s executives in early September and shared copies with The Boston Globe and WBUR public radio station . “Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is,” according to the petition. “The risk for Boston Dynamics is simply too great to continue with this deal.” Read full article Comments

title: Musk accuses Ukraine of violating Starlink terms with deadly drone strikes
raw_text: Elon Musk accused Ukraine of violating Starlink terms of service by using it for lethal drone strikes. Musk said Ukraine used the Starlink commercial service for offensive drone strikes. Musk's comment on Saturday came after SpaceX imposed a restriction preventing Ukraine from using the satellite technology on drones flying above certain speeds. One current and one former Ukraine official denied Musk's accusation and said previous limits imposed by SpaceX already prevented Ukraine's military from using Starlink in the way Musk described. Ukraine officials have accused Musk of throttling their use of Starshield, the military variant of Starlink that Ukraine has access to through a deal with the US government. title: Highway thieves are spoofing GPS to steal millions in data center-bound cargo
raw_text: Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment. NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts yet and reported that since June, thieves have “made away with more than $100 million in data center freight.” Here’s how they said thieves get away with it: First, thieves hack freight brokers’ accounts on shipment-listing websites and post fake shipments to lure real bids, then send a malicious link to any trucking companies that respond. Once victims click, thieves install software to take control of their accounts and start bidding on real shipments. Sometimes, a real delivery driver is hired to collect the cargo, unaware of the scam, and other times fake driver’s licenses are used to get accomplices hired. Either way, the goods are eventually transferred to a driver working with the thieves to resell the gear, and, in one of the largest thefts, tracking coordinates were spoofed to prevent digital monitoring. title: Some iPhone Duo screens are already failing
raw_text: The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple's first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn't going great. Despite the company's big talk about its "precision-engineered" hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device's impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use. The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin. Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo's screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself. Read full article Comments
